message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This study is built on a six-month pilot with 4,000 households across three deliberately mixed wards, so the projections are based on how Thornbury residents actually behave, not national averages. We measured participation and tonnage weekly, by housing type, and the results are encouraging: strong participation, consistent yields and 81% of residents rating the service good or very good. Crucially, participation held up across houses and flats, which means we can roll out a single, simple service across the district rather than designing separate arrangements. The financial analysis is complete and transparent. Every cost line is shown, from vehicles to liners, and the disposal saving uses our actual incineration cost and Brookfield's quoted gate fee, giving a net cost of about £490,000 that is fully covered by the provisional new-burdens allocation. Treatment is local, at a plant 14 miles away. The timetable works back from the vehicle lead time. I am confident the Council can approve this roll-out knowing it is evidence-based and fully funded.
</author>

<document>
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.
</document>
response:
# Review: Feasibility Study, Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection

**Overall:** The pilot design is sound, and the cost table adds up. The vehicle, crew and total arithmetic all check out, and the £490k net follows from the figures given. But three of the author's central claims are contradicted by the study's own data:
- The pilot shows participation in flats was **far lower** than in houses, not "broadly similar."
- The projection uses a **64%** participation rate that doesn't appear anywhere in the pilot results.
- Brookfield can take **only 1,800 tonnes** of the 3,290 projected.

Once corrected, the "fully funded" conclusion no longer holds.

## Major issues

### 1. Participation in flats was not similar to houses
From Table 1, houses participated at **66%** and flats at **21%**, less than a third of the rate in houses. Yet section 2 says participation was "broadly similar across housing types," and that claim is used to justify a uniform service with no separate approach for flats.

The data point the other way. Flats, about **10,400 households** district-wide, need a different approach, typically communal bins, bin-store access and targeted communication. This should be costed and planned, not dropped.

### 2. The projection uses a participation rate the pilot didn't produce
Section 3 applies **64%** participation. The pilot achieved **57%** overall. The pilot's 20% share of flats (800 of 4,000) also matches the district's 20%, so 57% is the directly comparable figure. Corrected tonnage:

| Basis | Tonnes per year |
|---|---|
| As stated (64%, 1.9 kg) | 3,290 |
| Pilot overall (57%, 1.9 kg) | about 2,930 |
| By housing type (66%/1.9 kg houses, 21%/1.4 kg flats) | about **2,870** |

That is roughly **13% less** food waste, and a correspondingly smaller disposal saving.

### 3. Brookfield can't take the projected tonnage
Section 4 states that Brookfield can offer **up to 1,800 tonnes a year** until 2029. The projection is 3,290 tonnes, or about 2,870 corrected, which leaves **1,070–1,490 tonnes** a year with nowhere costed to go. Despite this, the saving of about £243k assumes every tonne goes to Brookfield at £38.

The surplus would go to the plant 46 miles away, with an unknown gate fee and extra haulage costs including vehicle time, fuel and possibly a transfer arrangement. Separately collected food waste shouldn't simply go back to incineration. The author's claim that "treatment is local" is true for only about 60% of the projected tonnage.

### 4. The service is no longer fully funded
Taking only the corrected tonnage, and generously assuming every tonne still saves £74:
- Disposal saving: 2,870 t × £74 ≈ **£212k**
- Net cost: £733k − £212k ≈ **£521k**, which is just *above* the £520k allocation

Adding haulage and the gate fee for the second plant on more than 1,000 tonnes pushes the net cost further over. The stated headroom of about £30k was thin to begin with, and the allocation is described as **provisional**. The paper needs a funding gap scenario and a contingency.

## Other issues

5. **The cost table isn't "complete."** Lines that are missing or unclear:
   - **Spare vehicle:** Six vehicles for six rounds leaves no cover for breakdowns or servicing.
   - **Absence cover:** Agency staff for holiday and sickness across 12 operatives.
   - **Supervision and management**, plus the contact centre and dedicated phone line in section 6.
   - **Haulage to the second AD plant** (issue 3).
   - **Cost of capital:** The vehicles are straight-line depreciated with no financing cost.
   - **Ongoing liners:** Section 6 mentions only a three-month supply. Is there a continuing liner supply after that, and is it in the £88k?
   - **The £34k per operative:** Does it include on-costs such as employer NI and pension?

6. **The vehicle lead time is a schedule risk.** Ordering in December for March delivery assumes a three-month lead time. Lead times for refuse vehicles are often considerably longer, so this should be confirmed in writing with the supplier and a fallback stated, such as short-term hire. The rest of the timetable is also tight:
   - recruitment from February;
   - training in March;
   - delivering caddies to 52,000 households in a single month.

7. **The statutory deadline needs checking.** Section 1 cites the duty on English councils but not its date. The Simpler Recycling requirement for weekly household food waste collections applies from 31 March 2026, unless a transitional arrangement covers Thornbury. If not, an April 2027 start is already late, and the paper should address that directly.

8. **The pilot evidence is weaker than presented.**
   - **The pilot ran January to June.** It misses summer, when smell and fly concerns tend to reduce participation, and Christmas.
   - **The early-novelty effect isn't separated out.** Weekly data exists, so show whether participation stayed steady or declined over the six months.
   - **The 81% satisfaction figure lacks context.** It comes from "surveyed pilot households," but the response rate and the mix of participants and non-participants aren't given, and satisfied participants are likely over-represented.

9. **Check the incineration saving.** £112/t is the right comparison only if incineration costs fall tonne for tonne. If the contract has a minimum-tonnage or put-or-pay clause, diverting food waste may save less than projected.

## Suggested fixes

1. **Rewrite the flats finding** and include a costed approach for flats, such as communal bins and targeted engagement.
2. **Rebuild the projection** from the pilot's actual rates by housing type, giving about 2,870 t, and show sensitivity to participation.
3. **Add a treatment plan for the tonnage above 1,800 t to 2029**, with haulage and gate-fee costs, or secure more Brookfield capacity in writing.
4. **Complete the cost table** with the lines in issue 5, and recompute the net cost against the provisional funding, including a shortfall scenario.
5. **Confirm the vehicle lead time and the statutory deadline**, and add schedule contingencies.
6. **Reword the recommendation.** Instead of "fully funded" and "uniform," state the funding gap and the separate approach needed for flats.

The core case for the service is sound, and the pilot provides genuinely useful local data. The recommendation needs to reflect what that data actually shows.
